analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the Department of Energy and sells off its federal power assets, laboratories, and petroleum reserves.
analysis.headline: The bill to abolish the Department of Energy never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber, dying quietly after subcommittee referrals.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the Department of Energy as a cabinet agency. It would have moved nuclear weapons programs into the Pentagon, shut down or privatized national energy laboratories, sold federal power marketing administrations (the government entities that sell hydroelectric power, mostly in the West and South) to private buyers, and put the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and nuclear waste program under other agencies. It was introduced by Rep. Todd Tiahrt with 38 Republican cosponsors and referred to six House committees, but it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Buyers of the federal power generation and transmission assets — private utilities and energy companies — would acquire public hydroelectric and transmission infrastructure at sale. Buyers of naval petroleum reserves and privatized national laboratories would likewise gain. Taxpayers would receive one-time Treasury proceeds from the sales, though the bill also would have transferred federal electricity sold at cost-based rates to the market, which historically meant higher prices for rural and Western consumers — partially cushioned by a 10% annual rate cap that expires once prices reach market rates [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private buyers of federal power assets

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Secretary of Energy to sell federal power generation and transmission facilities to domestic buyers at the highest possible price, with proceeds deposited in the Treasury — a one-time windfall for federal coffers and a transfer of public assets into private hands.

It establishes a seven-member Energy Laboratory Facilities Commission empowered to recommend closure or privatization of national energy laboratories, with those recommendations taking effect automatically unless Congress affirmatively votes to block them.
It terminates DOE clean coal technology research and sunsets all DOE fossil energy and energy conservation research and development at the end of FY 2002.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers in regions served by federal power marketing administrations, who could face market-rate electricity prices after privatization; communities near national laboratories targeted for closure; and communities near defense nuclear sites, whose cleanup standards would shift to a Pentagon cost-benefit test [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: The 10% annual cap on rate increases for newly sold federal power assets ends as soon as the price reaches the regional wholesale market rate, so customers' long-term protection from price increases depends entirely on market conditions after privatization.

The bill moves defense nuclear cleanup decisions into the Department of Defense and requires cost-benefit analysis before remediation at contaminated sites, replacing the independent Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board's oversight — a change cleanup advocates at the time warned could slow or weaken environmental restoration at places like Hanford and Savannah River.

The Commission's laboratory closure and privatization recommendations would take effect automatically unless both chambers of Congress enact a joint resolution of disapproval within 45 days — an up-or-down, no-amendment process that makes stopping individual closures difficult.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill never advanced far enough for its merits to be weighed. Had it been taken up, its core idea — selling public power assets to private buyers and shrinking DOE — would have meant rate protections only until prices hit market rates, and much lower scrutiny of nuclear cleanup than the existing safety board provided.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees and various subcommittees, received an executive comment request from the Department of Energy, and then sat until the 106th Congress ended without any hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 29, 1999 with 38 Republican cosponsors and referred to six House committees, including Commerce, Armed Services, Science, Resources, Rules, and Government Reform.
In May 1999 it was referred to six different subcommittees and the House requested an executive comment from the Department of Energy; the record shows no hearings, no markup, and no votes afterward.
The Congress ended January 3, 2001 with the bill still in committee; it never reached the House floor or the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Department of Energy and its federal power and laboratory programs survive intact because the bill died; no assets were sold and no programs were terminated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Department of Energy and its programs

for.name: Rep. Todd Tiahrt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Department of Energy Abolishment Act on April 29, 1999.

for.name: 38 House Republican cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors including Reps. DeLay, Kasich, Coburn, and Paul

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors, including the sponsor, were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, and it never advanced out of committee.

industries.industry: Department of Energy and its national laboratories
industries.note: The bill abolishes the department as a cabinet agency, sunsets its research programs, and puts its laboratories on a path to closure or privatization. Its fate was the bill's central purpose.

industries.industry: Private electric utilities and power asset buyers
industries.note: Selling federal Power Marketing Administration generation and transmission facilities would create major acquisition opportunities for private buyers, who would then sell power to former federal-preference customers under only a temporary price cap.

industries.industry: Defense contractors and national laboratories (Sandia, Los Alamos, Lawrence Livermore)
industries.note: The labs' budgets would move under a new Defense Department Under Secretary, with privatization or closure on the table, but weapons-related work would continue under Defense rather than end.

Cleanup decisions at contaminated nuclear sites would move to the Pentagon with mandatory cost-benefit weighting, and the independent Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board would be abolished, reducing the outside scrutiny those communities have relied on.
